passages.t: Envoys from Babylon, and everything shown
passages.happening:
‘At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness and recovery’ (verse 1).

Hezekiah welcomes the envoys gladly and shows them everything in his treasure house, the silver, gold, spices and precious oil, and his whole armory. There is nothing in his palace or his kingdom that he does not show them (verse 2).

Isaiah comes to the king and asks where the men came from and what they said. Hezekiah answers, ‘They came to me from a distant land’ (verse 3), from Babylon. Isaiah asks what they have seen, and Hezekiah says they have seen everything; there is nothing among his treasures he did not show them (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Merodach-baladan, Marduk-apla-iddina in Babylonian records, was a Chaldean leader from southern Mesopotamia who seized the throne of Babylon and held it for about twelve years, from about 721 to 710 BC, before Sargon II drove him out. He regained the city briefly around 703 BC, only to be expelled again by Sennacherib. He spent much of his career organizing resistance to Assyria.

Many historians think his embassy was more than a get-well visit. It was a search for allies in the west. That would place the visit before Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC, and it would explain why Hezekiah showed the envoys his armory as well as his gold. He was showing a possible ally what he had to offer.

In Hezekiah's day Babylon was a restless province under Assyria, not a threat to Judah. The first hearers of this story, especially later ones, knew what Babylon would become.
passages.later: Chronicles adds a comment on the visit: ‘God left him alone to test him, that He might know all that was in Hezekiah’s heart’ (2 Chronicles 32:31).
passages.asks: Hezekiah showed the envoys everything he had. Ask what you are eager to show off, and to whom. And ask whether there is an alliance you are pursuing that God has not been asked about.

passages.t: Everything will be carried off to Babylon
passages.happening:
Isaiah says, ‘Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts’ (verse 5). ‘The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD’ (verse 6). ‘And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon’ (verse 7).

Hezekiah answers, ‘The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good’ (verse 8). For he thought there would at least be peace and security in his lifetime.
passages.hearers:
The prophecy looks past Hezekiah's day to a time more than a century later. In 597 BC Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem, carried off the treasures of the temple and the palace along with King Jehoiachin and his court, and in 587 or 586 BC he destroyed the city.

The chapter closes the first half of the book on a note that is not triumphant. The faithful king who prayed and saw Jerusalem delivered from Assyria cannot secure his people's future. What he showed off will be carried away. The very next chapter opens with comfort for a people in Babylon.

The narrator reports Hezekiah's inner thought, which leaves readers to weigh it.
passages.later: Kings records the fulfillment: ‘As the LORD had declared, Nebuchadnezzar also carried off all the treasures from the house of the LORD and the royal palace’ (2 Kings 24:13). Daniel's story begins with young men ‘from the royal family and the nobility’ taken to serve in Babylon's court (Daniel 1:3).
passages.hard:
Was Hezekiah's response in verse 8 selfish relief or humble acceptance?

Readers have taken it both ways, and the text leaves room for both. On one reading Hezekiah is complacent: told that his descendants will be taken into captivity, he is glad the trouble will come after he is gone. The narrator's report of his inner thought seems to invite that judgment. On another reading Hezekiah accepts God's word as just and sees the delay as mercy, as God delayed disaster after Ahab humbled himself and in Josiah's day. He calls the word good because it comes from God.

The chapter may be deliberately ambiguous, and these notes take no side. What is not ambiguous is the direction of the story: a faithful king could not secure his people's future, and the book now turns to what God himself will do.
passages.asks: Hezekiah was glad that the disaster would come after his time. Ask whether you think about the generations after you, or only about your own peace. And ask what you are building that will be handed on, and what will be carried off.
